blocks.text_original: ABOUT VCMI
blocks.text_normalised: ABOUT VCMI

blocks.text_original:
VCMI is an international initiative to drive credible, 
net zero-aligned participation in voluntary carbon 
markets. VCMI was established to help ensure 
that voluntary carbon markets make a significant, 
measurable, and positive contribution to achieving the 
Paris Agreement goals, while also promoting inclusive 
and sustainable development. The imperative of 
keeping global average temperature increase below 
1.5 degrees Celsius requires the world to avoid, reduce, 
and remove as large a quantity of greenhouse gas 
(GHG) emissions as possible, as quickly as possible.

to climate action while also supporting the 
achievement of the UN SDGs. VCMI connects with 
and amplifies initiatives that share this vision.

blocks.text_original: THE PURPOSE OF THE CLAIMS CODE
blocks.text_normalised: THE PURPOSE OF THE CLAIMS CODE

blocks.text_original:
Voluntary carbon markets have the potential 
to help fill gaps in financing for climate 
mitigation, enhance corporate efforts to 
transition to Net Zero and support the 
achievement of countries’ Nationally 
Determined Contributions and sustainable 
development objectives. They can also 
support and accelerate the introduction of 
robust, well-designed climate policies.
blocks.text_normalised: Voluntary carbon markets have the potential to help fill gaps in financing for climate mitigation, enhance corporate efforts to transition to Net Zero and support the achievement of countries' Nationally Determined Contributions and sustainable development objectives. They can also support and accelerate the introduction of robust, well-designed climate policies.

blocks.text_original:
However, this potential can only be realized if 
voluntary carbon markets operate with high 
integrity. This means that carbon credits 
must be generated by activities that truly go 
beyond business-as-usual and benefit host 
communities - the supply side - and that 
their use increases overall greenhouse gas 
mitigation rather than substituting for existing 
actions - the demand side. Without clear high 
integrity rules for both aspects, voluntary 
carbon markets will rightly continue to be 
viewed with suspicion, companies will be 
afraid to invest, and their potential will be lost.

Without clear high integrity rules for both aspects, voluntary carbon markets will rightly continue to be viewed with suspicion, companies will be afraid to invest, and their potential will be lost.

blocks.text_original:
The Claims Code addresses ′integrity on′ the 
demand side by guiding companies and other 
non-state actors on how they can credibly 
make voluntary use of carbon credits as part 
of their climate commitments and on the 
associated claims they can make regarding 
the use of those credits.  It provides clarity, 
transparency and consistency on what these 
commitments and claims mean and will 
give confidence to all those engaging with 
voluntary carbon markets.

blocks.text_original:
On behalf of the Voluntary Carbon Markets 
Integrity Initiative (VCMI) Steering Committee 
and Secretariat, we are pleased to present 
this Claims Code of Practice on the voluntary 
use of carbon credits. Such guidance is 
essential to ensure the integrity of voluntary 
carbon markets. Integrity underpins trust 
and trust will underpin the growth, in the 
short, medium and long term, of high-value 
and purposeful voluntary carbon markets 
– markets that can make a meaningful 
contribution to the Paris Agreement goals 
while at the same time contributing to the UN 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

blocks.text_original:
A climate transition plan, sometimes referred to as net zero transition plans, is an entity’s overall strategy 
that lays out the entity’s targets, actions or resources for its transition towards a lower-carbon economy, 
including actions such as reducing its greenhouse gas emissions8. Generally spanning several decades, 
it outlines a set of objectives, policies, steps and firm plans to take to reach net zero. At the corporate 
level, a transition plan helps a company demonstrate accountability and transparency by translating net 
zero commitments into actionable steps. However, there is no universal definition of a ‘transition plan’, 
and the specific elements vary across institutions, jurisdictions, and individual companies.

or retired by means of an electronic registry.

blocks.text_original:
Carbon Offsetting and 
Reduction Scheme 
for International 
Aviation (CORSIA)
blocks.text_normalised: Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA)

blocks.text_original:
A global market-based mechanism, adopted by the International Civil Aviation 
Organization (ICAO) in 2016, to address CO2 emissions from international aviation. 
CORSIA is the first global market-based measure for an individual sector. It 
pursues a cooperative approach, involving governments, industry, and international 
organizations, that attempts to replace a patchwork of national or regional regulatory 
initiatives. CORSIA aims to stabilize, from 2021, international civil aviation CO2 
emissions at 2019 levels, including through the use of carbon credits that are 
determined by ICAO to meet the CORSIA Emissions Units Eligibility Criteria. (For 
additional information, see ICAO, 2021).
blocks.text_normalised: A global market-based mechanism, adopted by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) in 2016, to address CO2 emissions from international aviation. CORSIA is the first global market-based measure for an individual sector. It pursues a cooperative approach, involving governments, industry, and international organizations, that attempts to replace a patchwork of national or regional regulatory initiatives. CORSIA aims to stabilize, from 2021, international civil aviation CO2 emissions at 2019 levels, including through the use of carbon credits that are determined by ICAO to meet the CORSIA Emissions Units Eligibility Criteria. (For additional information, see ICAO, 2021).

blocks.text_original: Claim
blocks.text_normalised: Claim

blocks.text_original:
A message used to describe or promote a product, process, business, or service with 
respect to its sustainability attributes or credentials (ISEAL, 2015).
blocks.text_normalised: A message used to describe or promote a product, process, business, or service with respect to its sustainability attributes or credentials (ISEAL, 2015).

blocks.text_original: Compensation claim
blocks.text_normalised: Compensation claim

blocks.text_original:
A claim that a company which is investing in BVCM might make that:
•	
Coveys to audiences that it delivered BVCM proportionate to a stated 
percentage of unabated value chain emissions;
•	
Seeks to convey that the BVCM outcomes are counterbalancing those unabated 
value chain emissions;
•	
Is based on the application of the tonne-for-tonne method to determine the 
nature and scale of the commitment to BVCM.

blocks.text_original: Contribution claim
blocks.text_normalised: Contribution claim

blocks.text_original:
A claim that a company which is investing in BVCM might make that:
•	
Represents support or finance to actions beyond the company's value chain 
(including collective action) with an expected climate mitigation outcome (where 
the actions are relevant to the expected performance outcome);
•	
Does not imply that the BVCM outcomes are netting out or counterbalancing 
the claimants' remaining value chain emissions, but instead are communicated 
as a contribution to global climate change mitigation efforts or even the efforts 
of a country;
•	
Is not defined by any particular method for determining the nature and scale of 
the commitment to BVCM (SBTi, 2023).

blocks.text_original:
(Climate) contribution 
approach
blocks.text_normalised: (Climate) contribution approach

blocks.text_original:
An approach where a company purchases or invests in carbon credits or other form 
of beyond value chain mitigation (BVCM). In a contribution approach, retired carbon 
credits are not counted towards, nor represent compensation for, a company’s 
remaining value chain emissions. The retirement of these carbon credits represents 
a contribution to overall global efforts to mitigate climate change. Both money-for-
tonne and tonne-for-tonne approaches can both be contribution approaches if 
companies are using contribution claims.
blocks.text_normalised: An approach where a company purchases or invests in carbon credits or other form of beyond value chain mitigation (BVCM). In a contribution approach, retired carbon credits are not counted towards, nor represent compensation for, a company's remaining value chain emissions. The retirement of these carbon credits represents a contribution to overall global efforts to mitigate climate change. Both money-for-tonne and tonne-for-tonne approaches can both be contribution approaches if companies are using contribution claims.

blocks.text_original:
Corresponding 
adjustment
blocks.text_normalised: Corresponding adjustment

blocks.text_original:
An accounting rule under the Paris Agreement’s Article 6 to ensure that, when a 
country authorizes and first transfers a mitigation outcome, emissions reductions or 
removals are not counted by the country that agreed to transfer it (WRI, 2019).
blocks.text_normalised: An accounting rule under the Paris Agreement's Article 6 to ensure that, when a country authorizes and first transfers a mitigation outcome, emissions reductions or removals are not counted by the country that agreed to transfer it (WRI, 2019).

blocks.text_original: Decarbonization
blocks.text_normalised: Decarbonization

blocks.text_original: The measures through which an entity reduces or avoids its GHG emissions.
blocks.text_normalised: The measures through which an entity reduces or avoids its GHG emissions.

blocks.text_original: Double counting
blocks.text_normalised: Double counting

blocks.text_original:
A situation in which a single greenhouse gas emission reduction or removal is 
counted by more than one Party toward achieving its Nationally Determined 
Contribution.

Free Prior and Informed 
Consent (FPIC)
blocks.text_normalised: Free Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC)

blocks.text_original:
Consent for any project, plan, or action given in advance and independently decided 
upon, based on accurate, timely, and sufficient information provided in a culturally 
appropriate way.

blocks.text_original:
Greenhouse Gas 
Protocol
blocks.text_normalised: Greenhouse Gas Protocol

blocks.text_original:
The Greenhouse Gas Protocol provides a comprehensive global standardized 
framework to measure and manage GHG emissions from private and public sector 
operations, value chains, and mitigation actions. Building on a 20-year partnership 
between the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for 
Sustainable Development, the GHG Protocol enables consistent and robust GHG 
accounting across entities. (For additional information, see GHG Protocol).

Building on a 20-year partnership between the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development, the GHG Protocol enables consistent and robust GHG accounting across entities. (For additional information, see GHG Protocol).

Integrity Council for 
the Voluntary Carbon 
Market (ICVCM)
blocks.text_normalised: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM)

blocks.text_original:
An independent governance body that is developing and enforcing a set of Core 
Carbon Principles (CCPs) that establishes a new threshold standard for high-quality 
carbon credits in the voluntary carbon market. The ICVCM will oversee a process to 
determine the Eligibility of carbon-crediting programs as well as which carbon credit 
Categories will become CCP-Approved. (For additional information, see ICVCM, 2023).

The ICVCM will oversee a process to determine the Eligibility of carbon-crediting programs as well as which carbon credit Categories will become CCP-Approved. blocks.text_original: Leakage
blocks.text_normalised: Leakage

blocks.text_original:
When a carbon crediting project or program does not halt emission-generating 
activities, but instead displaces them outside the project or program boundary.
blocks.text_normalised: When a carbon crediting project or program does not halt emission-generating activities, but instead displaces them outside the project or program boundary.

blocks.text_original:
Long-term net 
zero target
blocks.text_normalised: Long-term net zero target

blocks.text_original:
A company commitment to reduce emissions across its value chain (scopes 1, 2 
and 3) to zero, or to a residual level aligned with global net zero, no later than mid-
century. All residual emissions are balanced out by permanent removals (including 
high-quality removal carbon credits).
blocks.text_normalised: A company commitment to reduce emissions across its value chain (scopes 1, 2 and 3) to zero, or to a residual level aligned with global net zero, no later than mid-century. All residual emissions are balanced out by permanent removals (including high-quality removal carbon credits).

blocks.text_original: Mitigation contribution
blocks.text_normalised: Mitigation contribution

blocks.text_original:
Credits that are not authorized for transfer to be used against the NDC of another 
country, or for other international mitigation purposes, i.e., a credit generated through 
Article 6.4 to which a host country will not apply a corresponding adjustment.
blocks.text_normalised: Credits that are not authorized for transfer to be used against the NDC of another country, or for other international mitigation purposes, i.e., a credit generated through Article 6.4 to which a host country will not apply a corresponding adjustment.

blocks.text_original: Mitigation hierarchy
blocks.text_normalised: Mitigation hierarchy

blocks.text_original:
Prioritized steps to limit negative impacts, as much as possible, through mitigation 
(or reduction), restoration, and beyond value chain mitigation (WWF, 2020).
blocks.text_normalised: Prioritized steps to limit negative impacts, as much as possible, through mitigation (or reduction), restoration, and beyond value chain mitigation (WWF, 2020).

blocks.text_original: Mitigation outcome
blocks.text_normalised: Mitigation outcome

blocks.text_original:
An ex-post emission reduction or removal of GHGs determined by quantifying a 
baseline for emissions within a given boundary and then measuring how much 
a given intervention avoids, reduces, or removes and sequesters carbon from 
the atmosphere. A mitigation outcome can then be unitized and, in some cases, 
serialized for it to be traded as a carbon credit or offset.
blocks.text_normalised: An ex-post emission reduction or removal of GHGs determined by quantifying a baseline for emissions within a given boundary and then measuring how much a given intervention avoids, reduces, or removes and sequesters carbon from the atmosphere. A mitigation outcome can then be unitized and, in some cases, serialized for it to be traded as a carbon credit or offset.

blocks.text_original:
Money-for-money 
approach
blocks.text_normalised: Money-for-money approach

blocks.text_original:
A method for determining the nature and scale of a company's commitment to 
beyond value chain. In addition to delivering on its science-based target (covering 
value chain emissions), a company would allocate a share of revenues or profit 
towards financing climate mitigation beyond the value chain. The volume of finance 
deployed towards BVCM would be determined by the chosen denominator (e.g. 
profit or revenue) and the chosen percentage (SBTi, 2023).
blocks.text_normalised: A method for determining the nature and scale of a company's commitment to beyond value chain. In addition to delivering on its science-based target (covering value chain emissions), a company would allocate a share of revenues or profit towards financing climate mitigation beyond the value chain. The volume of finance deployed towards BVCM would be determined by the chosen denominator (e.g. profit or revenue) and the chosen percentage (SBTi, 2023).

blocks.text_original:
Money-for-tonne 
approach
blocks.text_normalised: Money-for-tonne approach

blocks.text_original:
A method for determining the nature and scale of a company's commitment to 
beyond value chain. In addition to delivering on its science-based targets (covering 
value chain mitigation), a company would channel finance into BVCM based on 
predefined price of unabated greenhouse gas emitted by that company in a defined 
period (e.g. in a given year or since the inception of the company). The volume of 
finance deployed towards BVCM would be determined by the chosen cost of carbon 
(e.g. a cost of carbon or otherwise) and the unabated emissions in that defined 
period (SBTi, 2023).
blocks.text_normalised: A method for determining the nature and scale of a company's commitment to beyond value chain. In addition to delivering on its science-based targets (covering value chain mitigation), a company would channel finance into BVCM based on predefined price of unabated greenhouse gas emitted by that company in a defined period (e.g. in a given year or since the inception of the company). The volume of finance deployed towards BVCM would be determined by the chosen cost of carbon (e.g. a cost of carbon or otherwise) and the unabated emissions in that defined period (SBTi, 2023).

blocks.text_original:
Nationally determined 
contributions (NDCs)
blocks.text_normalised: Nationally determined contributions (NDCs)

blocks.text_original:
The national climate plan put forward by a Party to the Paris Agreement, including 
climate-related targets, policies and measures the government aims to implement 
in response to climate change and as a contribution to global climate action 
(UNFCCC, 2015).
blocks.text_normalised: The national climate plan put forward by a Party to the Paris Agreement, including climate-related targets, policies and measures the government aims to implement in response to climate change and as a contribution to global climate action (UNFCCC, 2015).

blocks.text_original:
Near-term science-
based target
blocks.text_normalised: Near-term science-based target

blocks.text_original:
GHG emission reduction targets set within the next five to 10 years to reduce 
emissions in line with what the latest climate science deems is necessary to limit 
global warming to pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (SBTi, 2023).
blocks.text_normalised: GHG emission reduction targets set within the next five to 10 years to reduce emissions in line with what the latest climate science deems is necessary to limit global warming to pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (SBTi, 2023).

blocks.text_original: Negative emissions
blocks.text_normalised: Negative emissions

blocks.text_original: The emissions level beyond net zero where removals exceed emissions.
blocks.text_normalised: The emissions level beyond net zero where removals exceed emissions.

blocks.text_original: Net zero
blocks.text_normalised: Net zero

blocks.text_original:
Net zero emissions are achieved when anthropogenic GHG emissions in the 
atmosphere are balanced globally by anthropogenic removals over a specified period 
(as defined by the IPCC’s AR6 report and adopted by VCMI).
blocks.text_normalised: Net zero emissions are achieved when anthropogenic GHG emissions in the atmosphere are balanced globally by anthropogenic removals over a specified period (as defined by the IPCC's AR6 report and adopted by VCMI).

blocks.text_original: On track
blocks.text_normalised: On track

blocks.text_original:
In VCMI’s Foundational Criteria, where a company is taking sufficient measures 
to reduce emissions in comparison to the base year to meet its next near-term 
target, with appropriate governance structures to decarbonize, and is appropriately 
apportioning funding to finance the company’s decarbonization.

blocks.text_original: Permanence
blocks.text_normalised: Permanence

blocks.text_original:
The capacity of reduced, avoided, or removed emissions to not re-enter the 
atmosphere. In practical terms, this means giving the purchaser of a carbon credit 
confidence that declared emission reductions will not be reversed by a future event 
(for example, that the forest planted to absorb a certain amount of emissions will not 
be cut down or be set on fire) (WRI, 2010).
blocks.text_normalised: The capacity of reduced, avoided, or removed emissions to not re-enter the atmosphere. In practical terms, this means giving the purchaser of a carbon credit confidence that declared emission reductions will not be reversed by a future event (for example, that the forest planted to absorb a certain amount of emissions will not be cut down or be set on fire) (WRI, 2010).

blocks.text_original: Remaining emissions
blocks.text_normalised: Remaining emissions

blocks.text_original:
Emissions that remain in a given year as a company progresses towards the delivery 
of its near- and long-term targets (SBTi, 2023).
blocks.text_normalised: Emissions that remain in a given year as a company progresses towards the delivery of its near-and long-term targets (SBTi, 2023).

dioxide removals)

blocks.text_original:
Anthropogenic activities removing CO2 from the atmosphere and durably storing it in 
its geological, terrestrial or ocean reservoirs, or in products (IPCC, 2018).
blocks.text_normalised: Anthropogenic activities removing CO2 from the atmosphere and durably storing it in its geological, terrestrial or ocean reservoirs, or in products (IPCC, 2018).

blocks.text_normalised: Residual emissions

blocks.text_original:
Represent the emissions that cannot be completely eliminated or reduced to zero 
despite implementing all available mitigation measures contemplated in pathways 
that limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celcius with no or limited overshoot (SBTi, 2023).

Retirement of 
carbon credits
blocks.text_normalised: Retirement of carbon credits

blocks.text_original:
The transfer to a retirement account or the cancellation of a carbon credit. Once 
retired, the credit is considered ‘used’ and cannot be counted again toward a 
climate target. The owner of the retired credit can accurately claim to have reduced 
emissions and use those emissions to meet its climate commitments.

The owner of the retired credit can accurately claim to have reduced emissions and use those emissions to meet its climate commitments.

blocks.text_original:
Science Based Target 
initiative (SBTi)
blocks.text_normalised: Science Based Target initiative (SBTi)

blocks.text_original:
An initiative that mobilizes companies to set emission reduction targets based on 
climate science. A collaboration between CDP, the UN Global Compact, the WRI, and 
WWF, the SBTi defines and promotes best practice in science-based target setting, 
offers resources and guidance to reduce barriers to adoption, and independently 
assesses and approves companies’ targets. Adopting an SBTi-approved target is 
one of the We Mean Business Coalition commitments (For additional information, 
see SBTi, 2023).
blocks.text_normalised: An initiative that mobilizes companies to set emission reduction targets based on climate science. A collaboration between CDP, the UN Global Compact, the WRI, and WWF, the SBTi defines and promotes best practice in science-based target setting, offers resources and guidance to reduce barriers to adoption, and independently assesses and approves companies' targets. Adopting an SBTi-approved target is one of the We Mean Business Coalition commitments (For additional information, see SBTi, 2023).

blocks.text_original:
Science-based/
aligned target
blocks.text_normalised: Science-based/ aligned target

blocks.text_original:
A target that is in line with the latest climate science consensus on safe upper 
limits for global warming. Alignment with an IPCC model pathway of CO2 emission 
reductions that limits global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius with no or limited 
overshoot is the ultimate objective (SBTi, 2023). ‘Science-based’ is used when 
adhering to SBTi’s standards, while ‘science-aligned’ may not necessarily follow 
SBTi’s standards.

Alignment with an IPCC model pathway of CO2 emission reductions that limits global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius with no or limited overshoot is the ultimate objective (SBTi, 2023). 'Science-based' is used when adhering to SBTi's standards, while 'science-aligned' may not necessarily follow SBTi's standards.

blocks.text_original:
Scopes 1, 2, and 
3 emissions
blocks.text_normalised: Scopes 1, 2, and 3 emissions

blocks.text_original:
Scope 1 emissions are emissions from operations that are owned or controlled 
by the reporting company. Scope 2 emissions are emissions from the generation 
of purchased or acquired electricity, steam, heating or cooling consumed by the 
reporting company. Scope 3 emissions are all indirect emissions (not included in 
scope 2) that occur in the value chain of the reporting company, including both 
upstream and downstream emissions.

blocks.text_original:
Tonne-for-tonne 
Approach
blocks.text_normalised: Tonne-for-tonne Approach

blocks.text_original:
A method for determining the nature and scale of a company`s commitment to 
beyond value chain. In addition to delivering on its science-based target (covering 
value chain emissions), a company would deliver mitigation beyond its value chain 
proportional to the climate impact of some percentage of the greenhouse gases 
emitted by that company in a defined period (e.g. in a given year or since the 
inception of the company). The volume of finance deployed towards BVCM would 
be determined by the price that a company pays per tCO2e of BVCM (in the case 
of carbon credits, this would be determined by market prices) and the percentage 
of unabated emissions that are being “matched" with BVCM in that defined period 
(SBTi, 2023).

In addition to delivering on its science-based target (covering value chain emissions), a company would deliver mitigation beyond its value chain proportional to the climate impact of some percentage of the greenhouse gases emitted by that company in a defined period (e.g. in a given year or since the inception of the company). The volume of finance deployed towards BVCM would be determined by the price that a company pays per tCO2e of BVCM (in the case of carbon credits, this would be determined by market prices) and the percentage of unabated emissions that are being "matched" with BVCM in that defined period (SBTi, 2023).

blocks.text_original: Value chain emissions
blocks.text_normalised: Value chain emissions

Emissions from the upstream and downstream activities associated with the 
operations of the reporting company. Scope 3 emissions include all indirect
